more.text: Resources (servers, storage, apps) delivered over the internet and billed by use. Service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS. Benefits: scalability and cost. Risks: shared responsibility, misconfiguration, and vendor dependence.

sides.text: A company wants to pay only for the computing it uses and scale quickly. Which model?

more.text: Cloud computing.
The provider supplies virtual machines, storage, and networks; the customer manages the OS, middleware, and apps. Most customer responsibility of the three models.

sides.text: A company rents virtual servers and installs its own OS and software. Which service model?

more.text: IaaS.

sides.text: Rent a platform to build and run apps

more.text: The provider manages infrastructure and runtime; the customer manages its apps and data. Developers focus on code.

sides.text: Developers deploy code to a managed runtime without managing servers or the OS. Which model?

more.text: PaaS.
The provider manages everything except the customer's data, users, and configuration. Examples: hosted email and CRM. Least customer responsibility.

sides.text: Staff use a browser-based email suite the vendor fully manages. Which model?

more.text: SaaS.
Public: shared provider infrastructure. Private: dedicated to one organization. Hybrid: a mix of on-premises or private and public. Community: shared by organizations with common needs.

sides.text: A group of hospitals shares a cloud built for common compliance needs. Which model?

more.text: A community cloud.

sides.text: Who secures what in the cloud

more.text: The shared responsibility model: the provider secures the cloud itself (physical, hypervisor); the customer secures what they put in it (data, identities, configuration). The split shifts toward the provider from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS.

sides.text: A customer's storage bucket is publicly readable. Whose responsibility is that?

more.text: The customer's. Configuration and data are the customer's side of shared responsibility.
Challenges: consistent security policy, identity integration, secure connectivity, data movement, and visibility across environments.

sides.text: A company keeps sensitive data on-premises and runs web apps in the cloud. What model is it, and what should it plan for?

more.text: Hybrid. Plan for consistent policy and secure connectivity.
Cloud and managed vendors hold your data or run your services. Assess their security, SLAs, compliance, and exit options. Their failures can become yours.

sides.text: A cloud provider outage takes down your application. Which risk is this?

more.text: Third-party vendor dependency, a risk to availability.

Infrastructure is provisioned through machine-readable files (Terraform, CloudFormation) instead of manual setup. Benefits: repeatability, version control, consistency. Risk: an insecure template spreads misconfigurations quickly.

sides.text: Servers and networks are deployed from version-controlled templates. What's this called?

more.text: Infrastructure as code.
The provider runs and scales code on demand; you manage the code and data. Less patching, but risks include insecure functions, over-permissioned roles, and limited visibility.

sides.text: Code runs only when triggered and the team manages no servers. Which architecture?

more.text: Serverless.
An app split into small services that communicate over APIs. Benefits: scalability and contained failures. Risks: more APIs to secure, more network traffic, and complexity.

sides.text: An application is split into many small services that talk over APIs. Which architecture?

more.text: Microservices.
Systems sit on physically separate networks and hardware, not just logically separated. The strongest separation for sensitive systems.

sides.text: Classified systems have their own cabling and switches with no link to the corporate LAN.

more.text: Physical isolation.
A system is completely disconnected from other networks, including the internet. Used for highly sensitive systems; data moves by removable media, which is itself a risk.

sides.text: A critical system has no network connection at all. What's this called?

more.text: Air-gapped.
Using VLANs, subnets, and firewalls to separate traffic on shared hardware. Cheaper and flexible, but misconfiguration can break the separation.

sides.text: Guest and corporate traffic share switches but can't communicate. How?

more.text: Logical segmentation (VLANs and firewall rules).
SDN separates the control plane from the data plane, so a central controller programs the network. Benefits: automation and agility. Risk: the controller is a high-value target.

sides.text: A central controller programs all switches and routers through software. Which technology?

more.text: SDN.
You own and operate the hardware and software. Maximum control, but you carry the cost, patching, and physical security.

sides.text: A company keeps all its servers in its own data center. Which model?

more.text: On-premises.
Centralized: easier management, policy, and monitoring, but a single point of failure. Decentralized: more resilient and flexible, but harder to manage consistently.

sides.text: Management is easy, but a single failure takes everything down. Which architecture?

more.text: Centralized.
Containers package an app and its dependencies and share the host OS kernel, so they're lighter than VMs but isolate less. Secure images, scan for vulnerabilities, and limit privileges.

sides.text: Apps run in isolated packages that share the host kernel. What is this?

more.text: Containerization.

sides.text: Multiple virtual machines on one host

more.text: A hypervisor runs several VMs on shared hardware, each with its own OS. Benefits: consolidation and snapshots. Risks: VM escape, VM sprawl, and the hypervisor as a single target.

sides.text: Many servers run as VMs on one physical host. Which technology?

more.text: Virtualization.
Internet of Things devices (cameras, sensors, appliances) often have weak default security, few updates, and long lifespans. Segment them and change default credentials.

sides.text: Smart cameras ship with default passwords and rarely update. Which category?

more.text: IoT. Segment them and fix the defaults.

Industrial control systems and SCADA monitor and control physical processes (power, water, factories). Availability and safety come first; often legacy and hard to patch. Isolate them from IT networks.

sides.text: A water treatment plant controls its pumps through a supervisory system. Which technology?

more.text: ICS/SCADA.
A real-time operating system guarantees tasks complete within fixed deadlines. Used in industrial, medical, and automotive systems. Security risk: limited resources for protections.

sides.text: A medical device must respond within milliseconds, every time. Which OS type?

more.text: An RTOS.
Dedicated systems inside larger devices (printers, cars, appliances). Limited resources, hard to patch, long lifespan. Mitigate with segmentation and firmware updates.

sides.text: A printer's built-in computer is rarely updated. What is it?

more.text: An embedded system.
Design with redundancy, failover, and no single points of failure to keep systems running. Measured as uptime, such as 99.99%.

sides.text: Two servers share the load so one can fail without downtime. Which goal?

more.text: High availability.
How reliably a system can be reached. Architecture choices such as redundancy, clustering, and multiple cloud regions increase it.

sides.text: Which design factor is improved by clustering and failover?

more.text: Availability.
How well a system absorbs failures or attacks and returns to normal. Built with redundancy, backups, and tested recovery.

sides.text: A system keeps working through a node failure and recovers quickly. Which quality?

more.text: Resilience.
Hardware, licenses, staff, and security. Cloud shifts capital spending to operating spending; on-premises costs more upfront.

sides.text: Which consideration pushes some companies to cloud instead of buying hardware?

more.text: Cost (capital vs operating expense).

sides.text: Speed of response to users and demand

more.text: Latency and performance. Edge and distributed designs improve it; centralized or distant hosting can hurt it.

sides.text: Users far from the data center see slow responses. Which consideration?

more.text: Responsiveness.
Ability to add capacity. Cloud and microservices scale quickly (elasticity); fixed on-premises hardware scales slowly.

sides.text: Traffic spikes during sales and resources scale up automatically. Which property?

more.text: Scalability (elasticity).

sides.text: How quickly and simply systems go live

more.text: Cloud, containers, and IaC make deployment fast and consistent. Complex or hardware-dependent setups are slower.

sides.text: Templates let a team deploy identical environments in minutes. Which consideration?

more.text: Ease of deployment.
Moving risk to a provider or insurer through contracts, SLAs, or insurance. It transfers some financial impact, not accountability.

sides.text: A company buys cyber insurance to cover breach costs. Which strategy?

more.text: Risk transference.
Snapshots, backups, IaC, and VMs speed recovery. Complex legacy systems recover slowly.

sides.text: A VM is restored from a snapshot in minutes. Which advantage?

more.text: Ease of recovery.
Vendors must supply patches. Unsupported or abandoned products lack them, leaving known flaws open.

sides.text: A product's vendor has gone out of business. What risk does that create?

more.text: No patch availability. Replace it or isolate it.
Some systems (ICS, medical, embedded, legacy) can't be patched easily. Use compensating controls: isolation, segmentation, monitoring.

sides.text: A factory controller can't be updated without halting production. What approach?

more.text: Compensating controls such as isolation and monitoring.
Systems need reliable power: UPS, generators, redundant feeds. IoT and embedded devices may have limited power for security features.

sides.text: Which consideration covers battery limits on small IoT sensors?

more.text: Power.
Available CPU and memory limit what security can run (encryption, agents). Constrained devices may not support strong protections.

sides.text: A tiny sensor can't run strong encryption. Which constraint?

more.text: Compute.

sides.text: Where devices sit in the network

more.text: Placement determines what a device can see and protect: firewall at the perimeter, sensors at key chokepoints, IPS inline. Wrong placement leaves gaps.

sides.text: An IDS sensor is placed where it sees none of the server traffic. What's the problem?

more.text: Poor device placement.
Network areas such as trusted (internal), untrusted (internet), and the DMZ or screened subnet. Traffic between zones is controlled by firewalls.

sides.text: Public web servers sit in a separate zone between the internet and the internal network.

more.text: A screened subnet (DMZ) security zone.
The total exposure: open ports, services, interfaces, users. Minimize it by disabling unneeded features and segmenting.
The attack surface.
Each connection (VPN, partner link, wireless) is a path to secure. Limit, authenticate, and encrypt it.

sides.text: A third-party link to your network is added. What should be considered?

more.text: Connectivity: secure, limit, and monitor it.
If the device fails, it passes traffic. Prioritizes availability over security. Example: a bypassed IPS, or a door that unlocks on power loss.

sides.text: A firewall failure lets all traffic through. Which failure mode?

more.text: Fail-open.
If the device fails, it blocks everything. Prioritizes security over availability. Example: a firewall that denies all when it crashes.

sides.text: A device failure stops all traffic to protect the network. Which failure mode?

more.text: Fail-closed.
Active devices can block or modify traffic (an IPS). Passive devices observe and alert without affecting traffic (an IDS).

sides.text: A sensor alerts on malicious traffic but can't block it. Active or passive?

more.text: Passive (IDS-style).

sides.text: In the traffic path vs a copy of it

more.text: Inline: traffic passes through the device (can block, but adds latency and a failure point). Tap/monitor: a copy of traffic goes to the device (no impact on flow, can't block).

sides.text: A device receives a copy of traffic from a SPAN port. Inline or tap/monitor?

more.text: Tap/monitor.
A hardened server that administrators connect through to reach restricted networks. Centralizes and logs privileged access.

sides.text: Admins must connect through one hardened host to reach production servers. What is that host?

more.text: A jump server.
Forward proxy: sits between users and the internet (filtering, caching, anonymity). Reverse proxy: sits in front of servers (load balancing, protection).

sides.text: A server in front of web servers shields and distributes requests. What type is it?

more.text: A reverse proxy.
Intrusion Detection System: monitors traffic or hosts for suspicious activity and alerts. Passive and detective; doesn't block. Network-based (NIDS) or host-based (HIDS).

sides.text: A system alerts on suspicious traffic but doesn't stop it.

more.text: An IDS.
Intrusion Prevention System: sits inline, detects malicious traffic, and blocks it. Active and preventive. Risk: false positives can block legitimate traffic.

sides.text: An inline device drops traffic matching an attack signature.

more.text: An IPS.
Distributes requests across multiple servers for availability and performance, with health checks. Can provide TLS offloading.

sides.text: Traffic is distributed among several web servers and failed ones are skipped.

more.text: A load balancer.
Devices or agents that collect network or host data (IDS probes, taps, log collectors) for analysis in a SIEM.

sides.text: Devices at key network points collect traffic for the SIEM. Which components?

more.text: Sensors.

sides.text: Limits which devices can use a switch port

more.text: Restricts a switch port by MAC address or number of devices, to stop unauthorized devices plugging in.

sides.text: A switch port shuts down when an unknown MAC address appears.

more.text: Port security.
A device must authenticate before getting network access (switch port or Wi-Fi), using a supplicant, an authenticator, and an authentication server (RADIUS).

sides.text: A laptop must authenticate through a RADIUS server before the switch port passes traffic.

more.text: Extensible Authentication Protocol: carries authentication methods in 802.1X (EAP-TLS, PEAP, EAP-TTLS, EAP-FAST). EAP-TLS uses certificates on both client and server.

sides.text: Which EAP method uses certificates on both client and server?

more.text: EAP-TLS.
Web application firewall: inspects HTTP and HTTPS traffic to block attacks like SQL injection and XSS. Works at Layer 7.

sides.text: Which device blocks SQL injection attempts against a web app?

more.text: A WAF.
Unified threat management: firewall plus IPS, antivirus, content filtering, and VPN in one device. Simple, but a single point of failure.

sides.text: One appliance provides firewall, antivirus, and content filtering. What is it?

more.text: A UTM.
Next-generation firewall: adds application awareness, user identity, IPS, and deep packet inspection to traditional filtering. Works up to Layer 7.

sides.text: A firewall controls traffic by application and user, not only by port. Which type?

more.text: An NGFW.

sides.text: Ports and IPs vs application content

more.text: Layer 4 firewalls filter on IP address, port, and protocol (stateless or stateful). Layer 7 firewalls inspect application data and context.

sides.text: A firewall allows traffic by port number only. Which layer?

more.text: Layer 4.

sides.text: Each packet alone vs tracking connections

more.text: Stateless: checks each packet against rules only. Stateful: tracks connection state, allowing return traffic for established sessions.

sides.text: A firewall allows reply traffic only for connections started inside. Which type?

more.text: Stateful.

sides.text: Encrypted tunnel over an untrusted network

more.text: Creates a secure connection across the internet. Types: remote access (user to network) and site-to-site (network to network).

sides.text: Remote staff securely access the internal network over the internet. Which technology?

more.text: A VPN.
Users reach internal resources from elsewhere via VPN, remote desktop, or zero-trust access. Secure with MFA, encryption, and least privilege.

sides.text: Telecommuters need access to internal apps. What should protect it?

more.text: A VPN with MFA.
Encapsulating one protocol inside another, such as GRE or IPsec, to cross networks securely. A full tunnel sends all traffic through the VPN; a split tunnel sends only corporate traffic.

sides.text: Only corporate-bound traffic goes through the VPN; the rest goes straight to the internet. Which setup?

more.text: Split tunneling.
Transport Layer Security: provides encryption, integrity, and server authentication for web, email, and other traffic. It replaced SSL.

sides.text: A browser shows a padlock for an encrypted connection. Which protocol?

more.text: TLS (HTTPS).

sides.text: Secures IP traffic at the network layer

more.text: A suite that authenticates and encrypts IP packets. Modes: transport (payload only) and tunnel (whole packet). Uses AH and ESP.

sides.text: A site-to-site VPN encrypts whole IP packets between gateways. Which mode?

more.text: IPsec tunnel mode.
Software-defined WAN routes traffic across multiple links (broadband, MPLS, LTE) by policy, with central management and built-in encryption.

sides.text: Branch offices use cheap internet links managed centrally by policy. Which technology?

more.text: SD-WAN.
Secure Access Service Edge combines WAN capabilities with cloud security (SWG, CASB, ZTNA, firewall) delivered from the cloud, close to users.

sides.text: A company delivers WAN and security services from the cloud to remote users.

more.text: SASE.

sides.text: Match the control to the risk

more.text: Choose controls by risk, cost, operational impact, and compliance, and layer them (defense in depth). Don't spend more on a control than the asset is worth.

sides.text: Which approach picks controls by weighing risk against cost?

more.text: Selecting effective controls through risk and cost analysis.
A network segment between the internet and the internal network that holds public servers. If they're compromised, the internal network stays protected.

sides.text: Web servers must be reachable from the internet without exposing internal systems.

more.text: Place them in a screened subnet (DMZ).
NAC enforces policy: authenticate the device and check its health (patches, antivirus) before granting access, or quarantine it.

sides.text: A laptop without current patches is placed on a restricted network. Which technology?

more.text: NAC.
HTTPS 443, SSH 22, SFTP 22, FTPS 990 (implicit), LDAPS 636, SMTPS 465 or 587, IMAPS 993, POP3S 995, DNS over TLS 853. Avoid HTTP 80, Telnet 23, and FTP 21.

sides.text: Which protocol and port should replace Telnet?

more.text: SSH on port 22.
Data governed by legal or industry rules: PII, PHI (HIPAA), card data (PCI DSS), GDPR-covered data. Breaches carry fines and notification duties.

sides.text: Patient records fall under HIPAA. What type of data are they?

more.text: Regulated data.
Secret information that gives a competitive edge, such as formulas or processes. Protected by NDAs and access control, not registration.

sides.text: A recipe kept secret gives a company a competitive edge. Which type?

more.text: A trade secret.
Patents, copyrights, trademarks, designs, and code. Legal protections apply; theft of IP is a major risk.

sides.text: Source code and patented designs are examples of what?

more.text: Intellectual property.
Court records, contracts, and privileged communications. Often confidential, with retention and discovery requirements.

sides.text: Attorney-client communications need strict confidentiality. Which type?

more.text: Legal information.
Bank accounts, payment cards, statements, and accounting data. Targeted for fraud; protected by PCI DSS, SOX, and other rules.

sides.text: Credit card numbers and account statements are which data type?

more.text: Financial information.

sides.text: Readable by people or only by machines

more.text: Human-readable: documents, text, images. Non-human-readable: binary, encrypted, encoded, or machine formats such as barcodes and QR codes. DLP and classification must handle both.

sides.text: A QR code or encrypted blob holds data people can't read directly. Which type?

more.text: Non-human-readable data.
Intended for public release, such as marketing material. Needs integrity protection but no confidentiality.

sides.text: A press release is posted online. Which classification?

more.text: Public.

sides.text: For internal personal or company use

more.text: Information about individuals or internal operations not for public release. Exposure could harm individuals or the organization.

sides.text: Employee personal details held by HR. Which classification?

more.text: Private.
A broad label for data whose exposure could cause harm. Handled with access controls and encryption.

sides.text: Which label covers data that could cause harm if disclosed?

more.text: Sensitive.
Disclosure could seriously damage the organization: contracts, strategy, trade secrets. Access on a need-to-know basis.

sides.text: Merger plans must be seen only by a small team. Which classification?

more.text: Confidential.
The strictest controls; limited to specific people, often with legal consequences if exposed. Above confidential in many schemes.

sides.text: Which classification applies to the most tightly controlled data?

more.text: Restricted.
Data whose loss or unavailability would halt the business or endanger safety. Needs the strongest availability and recovery protection.

sides.text: A hospital's patient-monitoring data must always be available. Which classification?

more.text: Critical.
Data on disks, databases, or backups. Protect with encryption (full-disk, database), access controls, and physical security.

sides.text: A stolen drive exposes stored files. Which state is the data in?

more.text: Data at rest.
Data on a network or between systems. Protect with TLS, IPsec, and VPNs.

sides.text: Credit card data is sent from a browser to a server. Which state?

more.text: Data in transit.
Data in memory or being processed by an application. The hardest state to protect; use secure enclaves, memory protection, and access controls.

sides.text: Data is being processed in RAM by an application. Which state?

more.text: Data in use.

sides.text: Data is subject to the laws of its location

more.text: Data is governed by the laws of the country where it's stored or processed (like GDPR). Affects cloud region choices and cross-border transfers.

sides.text: A company must keep EU customer data inside the EU. Which concept?

more.text: Data sovereignty.

sides.text: Where data or devices are physically located

more.text: Determining and limiting location, used for access decisions, compliance, and tracking. Can enforce geographic restrictions.

sides.text: Access is denied when a login comes from an unexpected country. Which control?

more.text: Geolocation-based restriction.

sides.text: Limit where data or access can be

more.text: Block access or storage outside approved regions to meet compliance and reduce risk (geofencing, region locks).

sides.text: A cloud service is configured to store data only in a specific country.

more.text: Geographic restrictions.

sides.text: Makes data unreadable without a key

more.text: Protects data at rest, in transit, and in some cases in use. Choose strong algorithms and manage keys carefully.

sides.text: Which method keeps stolen data from being read?

more.text: Encryption.
Verifies data hasn't changed and protects stored passwords. Not reversible.

sides.text: Which method checks that a file wasn't modified?

more.text: Hashing.
Replaces portions, such as all but the last four digits, so users see only what they need. Often used in displays and test data.

sides.text: A screen shows ***-**-1234 for a Social Security number.

more.text: Data masking.
Replaces sensitive values with random tokens; the originals sit in a secure vault. Reduces exposure and compliance scope.

sides.text: Stored card numbers are replaced with random tokens. Which method?

more.text: Tokenization.
Disguising data or code so it's hard to read or reverse-engineer. Weaker than encryption: it hides but doesn't strongly protect.

sides.text: Code is scrambled to make it difficult to reverse-engineer. Which method?

more.text: Obfuscation.
Keeping sensitive data in separate networks or systems limits who can reach it and contains breaches.

sides.text: Card data is kept on a separate network from general systems.

more.text: Segmentation.
Using access controls and least privilege so only authorized users can read or change data.

sides.text: Only finance staff may open payroll files. Which method?

more.text: Permission restrictions.

sides.text: Distribute traffic vs act as one system

more.text: Load balancing spreads requests across separate servers. Clustering links servers to act as one logical system with automatic failover and shared state. Both support availability.

sides.text: Several servers behave as a single logical system with automatic failover. Which technique?

more.text: Clustering.
A duplicate site with hardware, software, and current data, ready within minutes or hours. The most expensive option.

sides.text: A bank needs recovery within minutes. Which site?

more.text: A hot site.
Has hardware and connectivity but needs data restored and some configuration. Moderate cost and recovery time.

sides.text: A company accepts a recovery time of about a day with a mid-priced option.

more.text: A warm site.
Just space and power with no equipment. Cheapest but slowest, since everything must be brought in and set up.

sides.text: A company wants the cheapest option and can wait weeks. Which site?

more.text: A cold site.
Placing sites and data in different regions protects against regional disasters. Consider latency and data sovereignty.

sides.text: Backups are stored in a different region to survive a regional disaster.

more.text: Geographic dispersion.
Running different operating systems, vendors, or platforms so one vulnerability or failure doesn't affect everything.

sides.text: Using two different firewall vendors in series reduces what risk?

more.text: A single shared flaw. That's platform diversity.

sides.text: Using more than one cloud provider

more.text: Avoids lock-in and single-provider outages and improves resilience. Adds complexity in security and management.

sides.text: A company uses two cloud providers to avoid depending on one. Which approach?

more.text: Multi-cloud.
Planning (COOP) so critical functions continue during and after a disruption, including alternate sites, people, and procedures.

sides.text: A plan keeps essential services running during a disaster. What is it?

more.text: Continuity of operations planning.
Planning people, technology, and infrastructure to meet current and future demand, so a spike doesn't cause an outage.

sides.text: Which activity helps ensure systems can handle growth?

more.text: Capacity planning.
Staffing for operations and incident response, including coverage and skills. Too few people becomes a risk during an incident.

sides.text: An incident occurs and there aren't enough trained responders.

more.text: A people capacity shortfall.
Sufficient hardware, software licenses, and tools for the load, with room for growth.

sides.text: A licensing limit blocks new users during growth.

more.text: A technology capacity issue.
Sufficient bandwidth, power, cooling, and space to support systems and growth.

sides.text: A data center runs out of cooling and rack space.

more.text: An infrastructure capacity issue.
A talk-through of an incident or disaster with key people, with no systems affected. Low cost, and good for finding gaps in plans and roles.

sides.text: Managers sit in a room and talk through a ransomware scenario.

more.text: A tabletop exercise.
Testing automatic or manual switchover to a standby system or site to confirm it works as intended.

sides.text: A team shuts down the primary database to confirm the standby takes over.

more.text: A failover test.
A hands-on exercise that simulates an incident or attack in a controlled way to test people, processes, and tools.

sides.text: A red team runs a realistic mock attack to test responders.

more.text: A simulation.
Running systems or processes simultaneously to compare results and validate recovery or migration without affecting production.

sides.text: The recovery site runs alongside production to verify results match.

more.text: A parallel processing test.

sides.text: Local for speed, remote for disaster

more.text: Onsite: fast restore but exposed to the same disaster as the original. Offsite (or cloud): survives local disasters but restores more slowly.

sides.text: Backups are stored in another city in case of fire. Onsite or offsite?

more.text: Offsite.
Set by the RPO: how much data loss is acceptable. Critical data needs frequent or continuous backups.

sides.text: A company can lose at most one hour of data. How often should it back up?

more.text: At least hourly, based on its RPO.
Backups hold complete copies of data, so encrypt them and protect the keys. A stolen unencrypted backup is a full breach.

sides.text: A backup tape is lost. What would have protected the data?

more.text: Backup encryption.
A quick copy of a system or volume's state at a moment, enabling fast rollback. Not a replacement for full backups.

sides.text: A VM is rolled back to its state from this morning. What was used?

more.text: A snapshot.
Full: everything. Incremental: changes since the last backup of any type (fast to make, slower to restore). Differential: changes since the last full backup (a middle ground).

sides.text: Restoring requires the last full backup plus the latest differential. Which type is that?

more.text: Differential.

sides.text:
Three copies
two media
one offsite

more.text: Keep three copies of data on two different media types with one copy offsite. Add an immutable or offline copy as protection against ransomware.

sides.text: Which rule recommends three copies, two media types, and one offsite?

more.text: The 3-2-1 backup rule.

sides.text: Copying data to another location continuously

more.text: Data is copied to another system or site in real time or near real time for fast recovery and availability. It copies bad changes too, so it isn't a backup.

sides.text: Changes to the primary database are copied to a secondary site as they occur.

more.text: Replication.

sides.text: Log changes so they can be replayed

more.text: Recording changes in a journal so a system can recover to a consistent state after a failure by replaying or rolling back.

sides.text: A database uses a log of transactions to recover after a crash.

more.text: Journaling.
Fuel-powered generators supply power during extended outages, starting after the UPS covers the gap. They need fuel and regular testing.

sides.text: A data center needs power for days during an outage.

more.text: A generator.
Uninterruptible power supply: provides immediate battery power and surge protection, bridging to generators or a clean shutdown.

sides.text: Servers must survive a brief power loss with no interruption.

more.text: A UPS.

sides.text: Time to restore and data loss tolerated

more.text: RTO: the maximum time to restore a system after an outage. RPO: the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time. They drive site and backup choices.

sides.text: A company can tolerate losing at most 15 minutes of data. Which metric?

more.text: An RPO of 15 minutes.
